paragraphs: Detective Inspector Alistair Finch stepped into the suffocating silence of Lord Harrington's study, the scent of old leather and rain-soaked tweed heavy in the air. Outside, a tempestuous autumn storm raged against the gothic manor, but inside, time had frozen. The old lord was slumped over his grand oak desk, a single, dark stain blooming on the chest of his crisp white shirt, his hand still loosely clutching a fountain pen as if he’d been interrupted mid-sentence. The scene was almost peaceful, a macabre portrait of wealth and sudden, irreversible stillness.

Finch’s gaze swept the room, cataloging the details with practiced efficiency. A crystal tumbler lay on its side near the victim's elbow, a dark amber pool of what smelled like expensive whiskey soaking into a stack of financial reports. In the doorway, a young man stood shivering, his face ashen. He was impeccably dressed in a dinner jacket, a stark contrast to the grim reality before him. "I... I just came in to say goodnight," he stammered, his voice barely a whisper. "He's... my father. I'm Arthur Harrington."

A statuesque woman with silver-streaked hair and a face carved from ice appeared in the doorway, her silk dressing gown shimmering in the lamplight. Behind her hovered a portly, red-faced man clutching a brandy snifter, his breathing heavy. "Beatrice," the young man choked out, "Mother..." But the woman, Lady Harrington, only gave her son a fleeting glance before her gaze settled on the scene with an unnerving calm. The portly man, Elias Sterling, Lord Harrington’s long-time business partner, pushed past Arthur, his eyes wide with a frantic energy that seemed entirely out of place.

"He was going to ruin me!" Elias Sterling blurted out, his voice a hoarse, brandy-soaked rasp. He gestured wildly towards the desk, sloshing his drink onto the priceless Persian rug. "We had a terrible row, not an hour ago. He was pulling his funding from the merger, threatening to expose... certain discrepancies. The man was a tyrant!" He suddenly seemed to catch himself, his eyes darting between the detective and the stony face of Lady Harrington, a flicker of panic replacing his blustering rage.

Detective Finch raised a hand, silencing Sterling’s panicked backtrack. "I’ll ask you all to wait in the drawing-room," he said, his voice quiet but carrying an undeniable weight of authority. He gestured to a uniformed officer who had just appeared in the hall. "My constable will be with you shortly. Please, do not discuss what has happened." His eyes, however, never left the portly businessman. "You, Mr. Sterling," Finch continued, a glint of steel in his gaze, "will remain here with me. It seems you and I have a great deal to talk about."

Finch circled the desk slowly, his eyes fixed on the perspiring businessman. "A terrible row, you said. Did this row become physical, Mr. Sterling?" Elias mopped his brow with a silk handkerchief, his face slick with sweat. "Physical? Good heavens, no! We shouted, yes. I may have... slammed my fist on the desk. But I wouldn't lay a hand on him. I left. I went straight to the liquor cabinet in the drawing-room to pour myself a drink and cool down." Finch’s gaze dropped to Sterling's right hand, where a fresh, angry red scratch ran across his knuckles, a small, damning detail against his pale, fleshy skin.

"And your hand?" Finch asked, his voice deceptively mild as he gestured towards the scratch. Sterling flinched, looking down at his knuckles as if seeing the mark for the first time. "Ah, that. It's nothing. When I... when I struck the desk in my frustration, I must have caught it on the edge of that damned letter opener. It's quite sharp." Finch’s eyes flickered to the ornate silver opener lying near the inkwell. It was a plausible, if convenient, explanation. As he leaned closer to examine the desk, another scent, faint and incongruous, teased his nostrils—the delicate fragrance of night-blooming jasmine, cutting strangely through the masculine aromas of the room.

Leaving Sterling to stew under the watchful eye of a constable, Finch made his way to the drawing-room. The air here was thick with a different kind of tension. Arthur Harrington was pacing nervously by the grand fireplace, while his mother, Lady Beatrice, sat ramrod straight on a velvet settee, her hands folded primly in her lap, her expression as unreadable as a closed book. She wore a perfume that was subtle yet distinct, a floral note that Finch immediately recognized as the jasmine he had smelled in the study.

Finch's attention settled on the matriarch. "Lady Harrington, my condolences. Can you tell me when you last saw your husband alive?" Her head tilted slightly, a gesture of cool curiosity rather than grief. "I saw him just after dinner, Inspector. He informed me he had business to discuss with Elias. I retired to my chambers to read. The storm gives me such headaches, you see. I only came down when I heard Arthur's dreadful cry." Her voice was a low, cultured monotone, each word perfectly enunciated, betraying no hint of emotion.

"And this business with Mr. Sterling," Finch pressed gently, "were you aware of its nature?" Lady Beatrice's lips thinned almost imperceptibly. "My husband rarely burdened me with the vulgar details of his financial dealings. I was aware they had a disagreement, of course. It's difficult not to be aware of Elias when he is displeased. He is a man of... considerable volume." The dismissal was subtle but sharp, a flick of a verbal stiletto aimed squarely at the portly businessman.

Finch then turned his attention to the son. "Mr. Harrington, you found your father. Was anyone else with you? Did you see or hear anything before you entered the study?" Arthur stopped his pacing, running a hand through his already dishevelled hair. "No, I was alone. I'd been in the library. I heard Elias shouting earlier, everyone in the house must have. He stormed out and I saw him head for the drawing-room. I waited a while before going to check on Father... I wish I'd gone sooner." His voice cracked, a raw edge of guilt and sorrow that felt genuine.

Later, back in the study, Finch found the preliminary report from the forensics team on his desk. Lord Harrington had been stabbed once, directly in the heart, with a thin, sharp object. The weapon was missing. The time of death was estimated to be between 9:00 and 9:30 PM, precisely during the period Elias Sterling admitted to arguing with the victim. Furthermore, a search of Sterling's pockets had yielded a small, mud-stained trowel, the kind used for gardening, its pointed end a perfect fit for the wound's dimensions.

When confronted with the trowel, Elias Sterling’s bluster evaporated, replaced by a genuine, sputtering confusion. "A trowel? Why would I... I was in the greenhouse earlier, tending to my orchids, it's my hobby! I must have forgotten it in my jacket pocket." His explanation sounded feeble, even to his own ears. "You expect me to believe you brought a gardening tool to a business argument that ended in murder?" Finch asked, his voice laced with incredulity. The circumstantial evidence was piling up, forming a neat, damning picture with Sterling at its center.

Finch requested a search of Sterling's room and the greenhouse. While the constables were busy, he returned to the drawing-room. Lady Beatrice was still seated, a portrait of composure, but Finch noticed a small, muddy smudge on the hem of her silk dressing gown, a detail that seemed at odds with her claim of having remained in her chambers. When he pointed it out, she barely glanced down. "I stepped onto the terrace for a moment, to see if the storm was abating. The wind must have blown some dirt from the planters." Her explanation was as smooth and cool as her demeanor.

The search of Sterling's room revealed nothing of interest, but the greenhouse was another matter. Tucked away behind a row of wilting orchids was a small safe. When the police locksmith finally cracked it open, it contained not cash or jewels, but a second set of account ledgers. A cursory glance showed they detailed a systematic embezzlement scheme, siphoning funds from the very merger Lord Harrington had threatened to torpedo. The motive was now undeniable; Sterling was not just arguing over funding, he was fighting to hide his ruinous crimes.

The case against Elias Sterling seemed all but sealed. He had the motive, a vehement and public argument with the victim at the time of death. He had a plausible, if flimsy, explanation for the scratch on his hand. Most damningly, a potential murder weapon, perfectly matching the wound, was found in his possession. Finch could practically hear the prosecutor laying out the open-and-shut case for the jury, painting Sterling as a desperate man pushed to violence to protect his web of lies.

Yet, something still nagged at Finch. It was the jasmine. Why would he smell Lady Harrington’s perfume so distinctly in the study if she had only been in the doorway? And the spilled whiskey—it had pooled on top of the financial reports, yet the papers underneath were bone dry. If it had been knocked over during a struggle with Sterling, surely the liquid would have seeped through more chaotically. It felt staged, a carefully placed prop in a meticulously constructed scene.

Finch returned to the study one last time, the others now confined to their separate rooms. He stood where Lord Harrington had sat, trying to reconstruct the final moments. He looked at the fountain pen, still clutched in the dead man's hand. On a hunch, he gently pried the fingers open. Tucked deep within the victim's palm, almost completely hidden from view, was a single, perfectly preserved petal from a night-blooming jasmine flower. It was small, delicate, and utterly out of place.

The pieces clicked into place with a sudden, chilling clarity. The jasmine, the smudge of mud on Lady Beatrice’s gown, her unnerving calm. She claimed she was in her room, then on the terrace. But the greenhouse, where Sterling kept his orchids, was also home to a magnificent collection of jasmine vines, their perfume notoriously potent at night. The muddy trowel wasn't Sterling's only gardening tool in the house.

Finch walked back to the drawing-room, the jasmine petal carefully preserved in his evidence kit. He found Lady Beatrice standing by the window, gazing out at the now-subsiding storm. "An interesting hobby, gardening," Finch began conversationally. "Mr. Sterling is quite fond of his orchids, he tells me. But you, Lady Harrington, you prefer the jasmine, don't you? The ones that bloom in the greenhouse."

For the first time, a flicker of something unsettled crossed her features. A tightening around her eyes, a slight compression of her lips. "I find their scent soothing, Inspector. Especially during a storm." Her composure was a fortress, but Finch had found a crack in the wall. "Soothing enough to take a stroll to the greenhouse to procure a cutting, perhaps? Just before you retired to your room to read?"

"My husband's affairs were... more vulgar than just business," she said, her voice dropping to a near whisper, the icy control finally beginning to thaw. "He kept a mistress. A young, foolish girl on whom he lavished a fortune. Our fortune. He was planning to change his will, to leave a substantial portion of the estate to her." She turned from the window, her eyes burning with a cold, long-nurtured fury. "He was going to humiliate me, to discard thirty years of my life for a passing fancy."

"So you went to confront him," Finch stated, the pieces falling into their final, terrible alignment. "After Sterling's noisy argument provided the perfect distraction. You came from the greenhouse, with a trowel of your own, one you disposed of later. You stabbed him. In his shock, he grabbed your hand, the one holding a sprig of jasmine, and a single petal fell into his palm. Then you staged the scene, knocking over the tumbler of whiskey to create a tableau of a struggle, a struggle that never happened."

Lady Beatrice's silence was her confession. The carefully constructed façade crumbled, revealing the raw, ugly motive beneath. Sterling’s financial desperation was the perfect cover, his blustering rage a convenient misdirection. He was a loud, obvious suspect, designed to draw all the attention while the true killer, silent and precise, faded into the background like a ghost in her own home. She had used his predictable anger as a shield for her own cold, calculated vengeance.

"Elias Sterling is a fool and a thief," she said, her voice devoid of any emotion save a profound, chilling weariness. "But he is a predictable fool. My husband believed he was the master of this house, of everyone in it. He failed to realize that the most dangerous threats are not the ones that roar, but the ones that wait, patiently, in the quiet shadows." As the constable moved to her side, a final, faint scent of jasmine seemed to rise from her silk gown, a spectral perfume of a crime almost perfectly concealed.

first_paras: Finch’s gaze swept over the three figures huddled near the grand, rain-lashed window, their faces illuminated by intermittent flashes of lightning. Lady Beatrice Harrington stood ramrod straight, her expression a mask of aristocratic composure, though her white-knuckled grip on the velvet curtain betrayed her inner turmoil. Beside her, her son, Arthur, paced like a caged tiger, his jaw clenched and a furious energy radiating from him that seemed entirely at odds with grief. The third man, Elias Sterling, the family solicitor, was a stark contrast to the Harringtons, looking pale and utterly shaken, clutching his leather briefcase as if it were a life raft in a stormy sea.

Huddled by the grand, unlit fireplace were the three people who had discovered him. Lady Beatrice Harrington, his wife, was a statue of perfect, silent grief, her face pale and her hands clutching a silk handkerchief so tightly her knuckles were white. Beside her, Elias Sterling, the family’s long-standing solicitor and confidant, stood stiffly, his expression a mask of professional solemnity. But it was the son, Arthur, who drew Finch’s attention. He wasn’t looking at his mother or the solicitor; his eyes were fixed on his father’s body, his jaw clenched and a muscle twitching in his cheek. There was no sorrow in his gaze, only a cold, simmering fury.

Standing by the rain-lashed bay window were the two remaining Harringtons. Lady Beatrice Harrington, a woman sculpted from ice, stared not at her deceased husband but at the swirling chaos of the grounds beyond, her expression unreadable. Beside her, her son, Arthur, fidgeted with the signet ring on his finger, his gaze darting between the detective and the slumped figure of his father. "He was a good man, Inspector," Arthur stated, his voice a fraction too loud for the somber room. "A pillar of the community. I can't imagine who would do this."

Finch's gaze lifted from the deceased lord to the figures huddled in the grand doorway, kept at a distance by a stoic constable. Lady Beatrice Harrington, a woman sculpted from porcelain and sorrow, pressed a trembling hand to her mouth, her eyes wide and vacant. Beside her stood their son, Arthur, radiating an entirely different energy. He was a tightly coiled spring of resentment, his jaw clenched and his knuckles white, his furious glare fixed not on his father's body, but on the opulent room itself, as if its very existence was an affront.

Finch’s gaze swept over the three figures huddled near the doorway, their faces pale masks in the dim lamplight. Lady Beatrice Harrington, the victim’s wife, was a fragile, trembling figure, leaning heavily on the arm of her son, Arthur. Arthur himself, heir to the Harrington fortune, wore a scowl of barely suppressed rage. Standing slightly apart was Elias Sterling, the family lawyer and the one who had placed the call to the station, his expression a carefully constructed wall of professional composure that seemed oddly out of place amidst the raw emotion.

Finch’s gaze swept the room, cataloging the details with practiced efficiency. A crystal tumbler lay on its side near the victim's elbow, a dark amber pool of what smelled like expensive whiskey soaking into a stack of financial reports. In the doorway, a young man stood shivering, his face ashen. He was impeccably dressed in a dinner jacket, a stark contrast to the grim reality before him. "I... I just came in to say goodnight," he stammered, his voice barely a whisper. "He's... my father. I'm Arthur Harrington."

"You knew him well, Mr. Sterling?" Finch directed his question to the agitated man, his voice a low, steady counterpoint to the storm outside. Elias Sterling flinched, his jowls quivering. "Knew him? We were partners for thirty years! But tonight... tonight we had a terrible row." He gestured wildly with his brandy snifter, sloshing the liquid dangerously close to the rim. "He was going to pull out of the Trans-Continental deal! The man was a fool! He was going to ruin me, ruin everything we built!"

"Who was the last person to see him alive?" Finch’s voice cut through the tension, sharp and authoritative. Before Arthur or Beatrice could answer, Elias Sterling took a step forward, his face flushed and glistening with sweat. "I was!" he boomed, his voice thick with a mixture of grief and fury. "We had a row, a terrible one. He was going to pull out of the merger, destroy everything we've built! I told him he was a fool, a stubborn old fool!" He pointed a trembling finger at the corpse, his knuckles white. "And now look at him!"

"I'll need you all to wait in the drawing-room," Finch said, his voice a calm authority in the charged atmosphere. But Elias Sterling seemed not to hear him, stumbling towards the desk with a desperate lurch. "The contracts," he muttered, his gaze fixed on the whiskey-soaked financial reports. "The merger... everything was riding on this. He was going to back out, I know it." He looked up at Finch, his face a mask of panicked greed, an emotion so nakedly obvious it immediately placed him at the top of the inspector's list.

"Please, nobody touch anything," Finch's voice cut through the tension, calm and authoritative. He gestured for them to move away from the doorway. While Beatrice and Arthur complied with a dazed obedience, Elias Sterling hesitated, his gaze locked on the whiskey-soaked documents. "The merger contracts," he breathed, his voice a hoarse whisper. "Everything was tied up in those papers. Everything." His eyes, Finch noted, were not on his dead partner, but on the potential ruin of their shared financial empire, now stained and possibly illegible.

"No one else is to enter this room," Finch's voice was a low command, cutting through the shock. He directed his gaze at the flustered business partner. "Mr. Sterling, you were saying?" Elias, however, seemed to have forgotten his initial panic about the body itself; his eyes were now locked on the papers scattered across the desk, darkened by the spreading stain of whiskey. "The merger," he breathed, his voice a hoarse whisper. "The final signatory papers for the merger... they were right there. Everything depended on his signature tonight." The raw, frantic greed in his eyes was unmistakable, a glint that seemed far more potent than any grief.

"He was going to ruin me!" Elias Sterling blurted out, his voice a hoarse, brandy-soaked rasp. He gestured wildly towards the desk, sloshing his drink onto the priceless Persian rug. "We had a terrible row, not an hour ago. He was pulling his funding from the merger, threatening to expose... certain discrepancies. The man was a tyrant!" He suddenly seemed to catch himself, his eyes darting between the detective and the stony face of Lady Harrington, a flicker of panic replacing his blustering rage.

As the others departed, a sheen of sweat broke out across Sterling's brow. "Now, see here, Inspector," he began, his voice losing its earlier bluster, "it was a simple business disagreement. Vicious, yes, but words only. I left him alive and well, I swear it!" While Sterling babbled his frantic denials, Finch's gaze drifted to the floor near the victim's chair. A small, glinting object caught the light. He bent down and picked up a heavy, ornate brass button, the kind often found on a gentleman's waistcoat. Without a word, Finch held it up, his eyes moving pointedly to the front of Sterling's jacket, where a single, identical button was conspicuously missing.

As the door clicked shut, leaving them in the morbid quiet of the study, Elias Sterling began to sweat profusely, his face turning a shade redder. "Look, Inspector, it was just business," he stammered, mopping his brow with a silk handkerchief. "He was being unreasonable, a stubborn old fool! But I wouldn't... I couldn't..." His words trailed off as Finch knelt beside the desk, his sharp eyes scanning the floor. Tucked almost entirely beneath the heavy velvet curtain, glinting in the lamplight, was the stub of a freshly extinguished cigar, the gold band bearing the distinctive crest of a brand Finch knew Sterling exclusively smoked.

With the door now firmly closed, the study seemed to shrink, trapping the two men with the silent third. Sterling mopped his brow with a silk handkerchief, his face a blotchy crimson. "Now, Mr. Sterling," Finch began, his voice deceptively mild as he slowly paced around the perimeter of the desk, "you mentioned a 'row'. Tell me about these discrepancies Lord Harrington was threatening to expose." As he spoke, his eyes caught a glint of gold on the dark wood floor, partially obscured by the leg of the victim's chair. He glanced at Sterling’s hands and noted that while the man’s right shirt cuff was fastened with an ornate 'S' initialed cufflink, the left one was bare, the fabric slightly frayed around the empty hole.

"So, Mr. Sterling," Finch began, his voice deceptively mild as he circled the desk, his eyes avoiding the victim for a moment to focus on the man before him. "Tell me more about these 'discrepancies'." Elias sputtered, wiping a bead of sweat from his temple. "It was nothing! A simple misunderstanding between partners, I assure you. Lord Harrington was... prone to dramatic gestures." As he spoke, Finch's keen eyes caught a glint of gold near the leg of the desk, partially obscured by the heavy drapery. He knelt, carefully plucking a small, ornate cufflink from the carpet with a gloved hand. He held it up to the lamplight. The intricate monogram was unmistakable: 'E.S.'. Elias Sterling’s face went white as a sheet.

Finch circled the desk, his movements slow and deliberate, his eyes fixed on the sweating businessman. "Discrepancies, Mr. Sterling? The kind that might interest the authorities?" he inquired softly. Sterling paled, his jowls quivering. "It was just a business disagreement, Inspector. Heated, yes, but nothing more. William... Lord Harrington... he had a temper. He provoked me." As he spoke, he nervously wiped his damp hands on his trousers, and Finch noted a small, dark smear on the right cuff of his tweed jacket, a smudge that looked suspiciously like gunpowder residue.

Finch circled the desk slowly, his eyes fixed on the perspiring businessman. "A terrible row, you said. Did this row become physical, Mr. Sterling?" Elias mopped his brow with a silk handkerchief, his face slick with sweat. "Physical? Good heavens, no! We shouted, yes. I may have... slammed my fist on the desk. But I wouldn't lay a hand on him. I left. I went straight to the liquor cabinet in the drawing-room to pour myself a drink and cool down." Finch’s gaze dropped to Sterling's right hand, where a fresh, angry red scratch ran across his knuckles, a small, damning detail against his pale, fleshy skin.

"Do you smell that, Mr. Sterling?" Finch asked, his voice low. He straightened up from the desk and took a slow breath. "Jasmine. It's quite strong." Sterling looked around blankly, his face a mask of confusion. "I smell nothing but dust and old paper, Inspector. My sinuses are all bunged up. Beatrice keeps the windows open for fresh air, even in this weather." Finch walked to the tall window behind the desk. It was latched firmly shut, rain lashing against the thick glass, sealing the room from the outside world and its scents. There were no flowers, no potpourri, nothing to explain the phantom perfume that lingered ghost-like in the air.

Finch straightened up, his brow furrowed. "Mr. Sterling, do you happen to know the source of that floral scent? Jasmine, I believe." The businessman looked bewildered, sniffing the air theatrically. "Jasmine? Inspector, all I smell is stale cigar smoke and my own impending financial collapse. Perhaps it's Lady Harrington's perfume lingering from earlier?" His answer was quick, almost too quick, and it did little to explain the scent's freshness. Finch made a noncommittal noise in his throat and turned his attention back to the desk, carefully lifting the corner of the whiskey-soaked financial report with the tip of a pen. The words "Sterling Investments – Final Notice of Withdrawal" were clearly visible in the Lord’s bold, angry script.

Dismissing Sterling to the drawing-room with a stern warning, Finch turned his attention back to the victim. He carefully lifted Lord Harrington's hand, the one not holding the pen. Tucked almost entirely from view, held loosely between the index and middle fingers, was a single, long strand of platinum blonde hair. It shimmered under the desk lamp, a stark contrast to the victim's own silver mane and a colour that certainly didn't match the silver-streaked brunette locks of Lady Harrington.

Finch crouched, his keen eyes scanning the floor around the desk. Partially obscured by the edge of the rug, a small, mother-of-pearl button glinted in the lamplight. He carefully plucked it from the carpet with his handkerchief. It was from a gentleman's waistcoat, of a style identical to those currently straining across Mr. Sterling’s substantial frame. "This room smells of jasmine, Mr. Sterling," Finch stated, his back still to the man. "An unusual choice for Lord Harrington. Were you or he expecting a female visitor this evening?"

"Do you wear jasmine, Mr. Sterling?" Finch asked, his tone dry. The businessman sputtered, his face flushing a deeper shade of crimson. "Certainly not! What a preposterous suggestion!" Finch straightened up, his eyes scanning the room once more. "And yet, the scent is quite distinct. Was there anyone else here in the study this evening? A woman, perhaps? Before your argument commenced?" For a moment, Sterling’s bravado faltered, his eyes darting towards the door, a flicker of uncertainty crossing his features before he regained his composure. "No. Absolutely not. Just Harrington and I. Perhaps it’s one of the maid’s cleaning fluids, or Lady Harrington passed by the door earlier. The scent lingers in these old houses."

Leaving Sterling to stew under the watchful eye of a constable, Finch made his way to the drawing-room. The air here was thick with a different kind of tension. Arthur Harrington was pacing nervously by the grand fireplace, while his mother, Lady Beatrice, sat ramrod straight on a velvet settee, her hands folded primly in her lap, her expression as unreadable as a closed book. She wore a perfume that was subtle yet distinct, a floral note that Finch immediately recognized as the jasmine he had smelled in the study.

"And you, Mr. Harrington?" Finch turned to the son, whose agitated pacing had not ceased. Arthur stopped abruptly, running a hand through his disheveled hair. "I was in the library, trying to read. But I could hear them arguing. Father and Elias. Their voices were raised... it sounded vicious. I couldn't make out the words, just the anger. It went on for what felt like an eternity before I heard the study door slam. A few minutes later, Elias stormed in here, muttering about ruin and betrayal, and poured himself that brandy." He gestured towards the drinks trolley where an almost-empty decanter stood.

"And your son, Lady Harrington? Where was he?" Finch turned his gaze to Arthur, who stopped his pacing abruptly. "I was in the music room," Arthur said quickly, his hands twisting together. "I was... practicing the piano. It helps me think. I was worried about Father and Mr. Sterling's argument. I could hear their raised voices from the hall, even over the music." He seemed earnest, his youthful face a mask of anxiety and sorrow, yet there was a nervous energy about him that felt like more than just grief.

"And you, Mr. Harrington?" Finch turned his attention to the son. Arthur stopped his pacing, running a hand through his already disheveled hair. "After dinner, I went to the library to catch up on some correspondence. I heard Father and Elias shouting... it wasn't unusual, they were always at loggerheads over business. I assumed it would blow over, as it always did. I didn't see Father again until... until I found him." His eyes were wide and earnest, but Finch detected a slight tremor in his hands that spoke of more than just shock.

"And you, Mr. Harrington?" Finch turned to the son. Arthur stopped his pacing, running a hand through his already disheveled hair. "I was in the library, trying to read. But I could hear them arguing. Father and Elias. Their voices were raised... it sounded awful. I couldn't make out the words, just the anger. It went on for what felt like an eternity before Sterling stormed out. I waited a while, then went to check on Father. That's... that's when I found him." His voice cracked, his youthful composure finally crumbling.

"And you, Mr. Harrington?" Finch turned to the son, whose agitated pacing had not ceased. "You found your father. Had you spoken with him earlier this evening?" Arthur stopped, running a hand through his already disheveled hair. "No, not since dinner. I was in the library, trying to distract myself. Father and I... we weren't on the best of terms. He disapproved of my... expenditures." A flush crept up his neck, a tell-tale sign of shame or perhaps something more. "I heard shouting from the study earlier. It was him and Elias, I'm sure of it."

"And this business with Mr. Sterling," Finch pressed gently, "were you aware of its nature?" Lady Beatrice's lips thinned almost imperceptibly. "My husband rarely burdened me with the vulgar details of his financial dealings. I was aware they had a disagreement, of course. It's difficult not to be aware of Elias when he is displeased. He is a man of... considerable volume." The dismissal was subtle but sharp, a flick of a verbal stiletto aimed squarely at the portly businessman.

Returning to the study, Finch found the forensics team dusting for prints. He paused by the open window, where the rain lashed against the panes. A muddy footprint, small and indistinct, was visible on the ornate carpet just below the sill, partially obscured by a heavy velvet curtain. It was a detail he hadn't noticed before, one that suggested an entry, or an exit, that wasn't the main door. The window lock was of a simple, old-fashioned design, easily jimmied without leaving much of a trace.

Returning to the study, Finch found the forensics team already at work. The lead investigator, a grim-faced woman named Davies, pointed a gloved finger towards a small, almost invisible detail on the carpet near the desk. "We found this, sir," she said, holding up a clear evidence bag. Inside was a single, long strand of dark, lustrous hair. It was clearly not from the grey-haired Lord Harrington, nor did it match the thinning, sandy-coloured hair of Elias Sterling. It was too dark for Beatrice, too straight for Arthur. It seemed another person had been in the room.

As Arthur spoke, Finch noticed something on the sleeve of his dinner jacket. A single, long strand of blonde hair, glinting in the firelight. It was a striking contrast to the dark, uniform hair of everyone present in the house. It was a small detail, easily overlooked, but to Finch, it was a loose thread, a snag in the carefully woven narrative of the evening. He made a mental note to have the constable collect it as evidence.

As Finch absorbed the son's statement, one of his officers entered the drawing-room and discreetly handed him a small, sealed evidence bag. Inside was a single, long strand of dark, lustrous hair, found clinging to the rough tweed of the victim's jacket near his shoulder. It was clearly not the grey, thinning hair of Lord Harrington, nor did it match the silver-streaked coif of his wife. It was the kind of hair that belonged to someone much younger, someone who wasn't currently accounted for in the grand, suffocating rooms of the manor.

A search of Elias Sterling’s guest suite, conducted with his flustered and indignant permission, yielded a damning discovery. Tucked away in the pocket of a tweed jacket hanging in the wardrobe was a small, pearl-handled ladies' pistol.
